title: Covering indexes and the index-only scan

videos.script: An index finds rows. Then, almost always, the server goes to the table to read them. {{twosteps}} For a query that asks for ten rows, that second step is ten more page reads, scattered across the table. {{scattered}} If every column the query needs is already in the index, the second step can be skipped. That is an index-only scan. {{ios}} There is a catch, and it is not in the index. The index cannot tell whether a row it points to is still visible to you. {{catch}} The table keeps a map of pages where every row is visible to everybody. VACUUM writes it, and every update erases part of it. {{vm}} In this lesson you watch the same index-only scan read three hundred pages, then eighty-seven thousand after one update, then four hundred after VACUUM. {{numbers}} Then you give lesson 2's customer orders query an index that carries the extra columns it returns. {{include}} It gets faster. And it costs something that no timing shows: six times the disk, and every update to an order now touches every index. {{price}}
